definition: Stupefy means to stun someone into dazed amazement.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stupefy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stupefy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The final round of the memory championship stupefied the audience: the winner recited two hundred digits without a pause.
A surprise merely catches you off guard — a friend at the door; it is far milder than stupefy, which stops thought altogether.
Astonish is strong — jaws drop — but it stops short of stupefy, which leaves its victims dazed, unable for a moment to think or speak.

Daze means to leave someone unable to think straight, whatever the cause — a blow to the head, exhaustion, shocking news. Stupefy is a daze with a signature cause: amazement so overwhelming it stalls the mind. Every stupefied person is dazed; a boxer can be dazed with no amazement at all.

Dumbfound means to astonish someone so completely that speech fails — the mouth opens and nothing comes out. Stupefy freezes thought rather than speech: a stupefied person can still talk, even babble, while the mind refuses to work. Dumbfounded is speechless; stupefied is dazed.

Stun means to shock someone so hard that reaction stops for an instant — bad news, a blow, a blinding flash. Stupefy lasts longer and centers on amazement: a stunned person recovers in a beat, while a stupefied one stays foggy long after the shock lands.

The auction house expected the little sketch to fetch a modest sum; the final bid — forty-two million — stupefied even the auctioneer, who stood with his gavel raised for a long, silent moment.
Stupefy is stronger than surprise or impress: it stuns the mind into a daze, so that for a moment thought and speech simply stop.
Its cousin 'stupor' names that same frozen state.
Use stupefy when amazement (or exhaustion, or a drug) genuinely stalls the mind — it is stronger than astonish and more physical than amaze.
In this unit it makes a tidy contrast with demystify: one word clears a head, the other stops one.

The eclipse reached totality at 11:14, and the town square went dark in the middle of the morning.
What struck the visiting reporters was not the darkness but the crowd: three hundred people stood stupefied, faces tilted up, minds visibly elsewhere.
People murmured, laughed in odd little bursts, repeated 'look at it' to nobody in particular.
But ask a question -- one reporter tried -- and the answer trailed off unfinished, as if thinking had been switched off while the mouth ran on.
Ten minutes after the sun returned, a barber said he still felt foggy, 'like waking from a dream that outweighed the day.'
